summary: Describes version 0.8 of the CyberCash credit card payment protocol, one of the few working Internet payment systems of its time. It is informational and documents a commercial system rather than an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: Before online shopping was common, one company invented a way to pay by card over the Internet without showing your card number to strangers. This memo describes how it worked.

questions: how did early internet credit card payments work
subtitle: A system for secure credit card payments over the Internet.

tldr.problem: In the early 1990s, using credit cards on the Internet was risky because customers had to expose their card numbers to merchants and network eavesdropping.
tldr.mechanism: CyberCash created a trusted intermediary server that holds encrypted card information, so customers never reveal their card numbers to merchants and merchants never see plain-text card data.
tldr.outcome: This was one of the few operational Internet payment systems of the mid-1990s, though it was eventually superseded by other payment methods.

today: RFC 1898 is informational, documenting a commercial payment system of the mid-1990s. CyberCash was one of the few working Internet payment systems at the time but was eventually superseded by other technologies like SSL-based card transmission and third-party payment processors. The protocol is historically important as an early example of solving the secure online payment problem.

sections.title: The Problem: Unsafe Card Payments Online
sections.content:
In 1995, the World Wide Web was new and nobody was sure how to handle credit card payments securely. If a customer typed their card number into a form, it could be intercepted by eavesdroppers. If the merchant stored the card number, it could be stolen from their servers. If the customer sent the card number directly to the merchant's bank, that happened over potentially insecure channels. CyberCash, Inc. (founded August 1994) set out to solve this with a general payments system that would keep customers, merchants, and banks separate and safe from each other.

RFC 1898 documents version 0.8 of the CyberCash system, which handles credit card payments only. The authors note it is informational, documenting a working commercial system rather than proposing a new Internet standard.
sections.eli5: In the early days, nobody knew how to safely buy something online with a credit card. You risked showing your number to hackers or to merchants you didn't trust.

sections.title: System Architecture
sections.content:
CyberCash created a three-party system. A customer downloads CyberCash software and registers a persona (a short ID with a check digit). A merchant sets up to accept CyberCash payments. A CyberCash server acts as a trusted intermediary between them and the banking system, handling encryption, authentication, and message routing. The server also connects to the customer's card issuing bank and the merchant's acquiring bank.

The design ensures that the merchant never learns the customer's card number (the bank may choose to reveal it later for specific reasons, but the protocol does not require it). The CyberCash server does not permanently store card numbers—they exist only briefly during processing, often in encrypted form within specialized cryptographic hardware.

Messages travel independently of the transport layer. CyberCash messages can be sent over HTTP, SMTP, or other protocols, so transactions are not locked to any single communication channel.
sections.eli5: Three parties: you (with encrypted card info), the shop, and CyberCash in the middle. The shop never sees your number. CyberCash hands it to your bank, which says yes or no.

sections.title: Security Mechanisms
sections.content:
CyberCash used several security techniques. Public-key cryptography (RSA) authenticated messages: customers, merchants, and the server each had a public-private key pair, and digital signatures proved who sent a message. Digital encryption (DES) protected sensitive data like card numbers. Hashing (MD5) created fingerprints of messages, allowing detection of tampering. Each persona was controlled by a private key kept encrypted by a passphrase. An emergency close-out passphrase could suspend a persona even if the private key was compromised.

The protocol was designed so card numbers were never visible in plain text in the CyberCash system except momentarily in secure cryptographic hardware. This greatly reduced the chance of card theft from the server.
sections.eli5: Strong encryption locked everything up. Your card number was encrypted so badly that even CyberCash couldn't read it except when needed for one transaction.

sections.title: Message Format and Transaction Flow
sections.content:
CyberCash messages have a transmission-independent format: a header identifying the CyberCash version, a transparent part (visible, unencrypted information), an opaque part (encrypted and signed financial information), and a trailer with a checksum. The transparent part includes transaction IDs, dates, and persona IDs. The opaque part holds card numbers, amounts, and merchant authorization details.

A typical credit card purchase works like this: the customer browses a merchant's website. When ready to pay, the customer clicks a CyberCash button. The merchant sends a payment request (PR1 message) listing the amount. The customer's CyberCash software adds the card number from their registered cards, digitally signs everything, encrypts it, and sends it to the merchant (CH1 message). The merchant adds authorization information, signs it, and forwards it to the CyberCash server (CM1 or CM2 message). The server authenticates both signatures, verifies the invoice matches both parties' views, and forwards the request to the acquiring bank. The bank processes it like a normal credit card transaction and responds. The server sends a receipt to the merchant, who forwards part of it to the customer.
sections.eli5: Messages go in pieces: who wants what (clear), secret stuff like the card (locked), and proof that it all matches. Everyone signs to prove it was really them.

sections.title: Message Types and Operations
sections.content:
CyberCash version 0.8 defined many message types. Registration messages (R1, R2) create new personas. Application retrieval messages (GA1, GA2) let customers download updated software. Binding messages (BC1, BC4) associate credit cards with a persona. Customer payment messages (PR1, CH1, CH2) implement the purchase request, card submission, and receipt flow. Merchant messages (CM1-CM6) handle authorization, capture, void, and return operations. Utility messages support pings, transaction queries, cancellation, and error reporting. Diagnostic messages let merchants and the server log information for troubleshooting.

Each message type specifies which fields are signed, hashed, or encrypted, and what operations the server takes on receipt.
sections.eli5: Different message types for signing up, buying things, refunding, and debugging. Each one specifies what gets locked up and what stays visible.

sections.title: Design Maturity and Future Work
sections.content:
The RFC describes a working system, not a proposal. Version 0.7 was used for testing and 0.8 was the first shipped version for credit card payments. The authors note that versions 0.9 and 1.0 were expected to add electronic cash capabilities and improvements to the credit card system. The security section acknowledges that the system uses encryption from leading security sources and commits to adopting new security technologies as they emerge.

A key design decision was that the merchant never needs the plain-text card number unless the bank chooses to provide it. This is a significant architectural difference from many later payment systems and reflects deep thinking about data minimization and security. The document includes detailed field-by-field examples of actual messages, allowing implementers to verify their understanding of the protocol.
sections.eli5: This was a working product, not a draft. They planned to add digital cash later. The whole design was built to minimize who sees sensitive information.
